hints.text: Use five heats, then race the five heat winners to rank the heats.
After the winners' race, only the top three from the fastest heat, top two from the second heat, and winner of the third heat can remain candidates.

solution.setup: Partition the runners into five heats of six and label each heat by finishing order.
solution.reasoning: Five heats rank runners within groups. A sixth race ranks the five winners. If A1 beats B1 beats C1, the only remaining candidates for second and third are A1,A2,A3,B1,B2,C1. Since A1 is already known fastest, race the other five once. That seventh race determines second and third.
solution.sanityCheck: Six races cannot suffice because after the winners' race several un-compared runners can still occupy second and third.

keyInsight: Each result eliminates whole dominance chains, leaving a small candidate frontier.
recognitionCues: Ranking without times requires exploiting transitive comparisons.
commonMistakes: Racing only the heat winners and overlooking strong runners behind the fastest winner.
followUps: How many races are needed for 36 runners and six lanes?

source.notes: Original variant of a publicly reported interview family associated with SIG, Citadel Securities.

verification.notes: Five heats, one winners race, and one candidate race are sufficient and necessary.

title: Thirty Runners, Six Lanes
problem: Thirty runners have distinct constant speeds. A track has six lanes and no stopwatch. What is the minimum number of races needed to identify the three fastest runners?
